description: Start with README.md to learn what ApexStore is: a full-stack monorepo pairing a NestJS v11 REST API with a Next.js 16 storefront. It documents the tech stack, setup and Prisma workflow, the full API reference, data models, and the frontend i18n and apiFetch conventions, giving you a roadmap for the rest of this tour.
title: Project Overview

description: The backend boots in src/main.ts, which loads dotenv, configures CORS for the storefront origin, and registers the global ValidationPipe, request logger, and success-envelope interceptor before listening on port 3002. AppModule is the composition root that wires together the Users, Auth, Products, Cart, Orders, and Prisma feature modules. Together these two files show how the application starts and how its parts fit together.
title: Application Entry Point

description: Building on the bootstrap from Step 2, every request flows through a cross-cutting pipeline before reaching a controller. The JWT auth guard verifies the bearer token and attaches the user, the roles guard enforces ADMIN-only metadata, the logger records each request, and the transform interceptor wraps successful payloads in a { status, data, timestamp } envelope. Understanding this pipeline explains both the 401/403 error shapes and the response envelope the frontend unwraps in Step 9.
languageLesson: NestJS guards, middleware, and interceptors separate cross-cutting concerns from business logic: guards decide whether a request may proceed, middleware observes the request/response cycle, and interceptors transform the payload on the way out.
title: Request Pipeline Security

description: Authentication is the only public surface: AuthController exposes POST /auth/register and POST /auth/login, delegating to AuthService for duplicate-email checks, bcrypt hashing, and credential validation. The login and register DTOs enforce email and password rules via class-validator, and the Passport JWT strategy turns the issued token back into a request user on later calls. A successful login returns an accessToken that the frontend persists and sends as a Bearer header.
title: Authentication Flow

description: With a token in hand, any authenticated user can list and read products, while creating, updating, and deleting require the ADMIN role checked by the Step 3 guards. ProductsController declares these routes and their guards, ProductsService implements CRUD over Prisma with not-found checks, and CreateProductDto enforces a non-empty name, positive price, and non-negative integer stock. This is the catalog that the storefront pages in Step 10 render.
title: Product Catalog Management

description: Each authenticated user owns one cart, managed through the /cart endpoints in CartController and the stock-aware logic in CartService. Adding items validates the quantity DTO and rejects requests that exceed available stock, while update and remove operations guard item ownership. The cart is the staging area that feeds directly into order creation in Step 7.
title: Shopping Cart Operations

description: OrdersController exposes create, list, and detail endpoints scoped to the current user, with CreateOrderDto requiring a non-empty items array of product-quantity pairs. OrdersService validates stock for every line item and then creates the order while atomically decrementing product stock inside a single Prisma transaction, returning a 400 on insufficient stock. This transaction is the most critical business invariant in the backend: it keeps inventory consistent under concurrent checkouts.
languageLesson: Prisma $transaction runs multiple reads and writes atomically: either the order and all stock decrements commit together, or the whole operation rolls back, which prevents overselling when two users buy the last unit simultaneously.
title: Transactional Order Checkout

description: The canonical Prisma schema defines User (with the USER/ADMIN role enum), Product, Cart, CartItem, Order, and OrderItem, including unique emails, the per-user cart constraint, and the cart-product uniqueness rule. The migration tables shown here create the User and Product catalog foundation plus the Cart and Order records that Steps 6-7 operate on, with join tables linking carts and orders to products. PrismaService, the shared client wrapper used by every backend service, is how the code from Steps 4-7 reaches these tables.
languageLesson: Prisma schema models map to PostgreSQL tables with relations expressed as foreign keys: @unique enforces one-cart-per-user and one-row-per-cart-product, onDelete: Cascade cleans up items with their parent, and migrations apply these definitions incrementally.
title: Database Schema Model

description: Crossing to the frontend, lib/api.ts is the single bridge to the backend: it persists the JWT from Step 4 and wraps fetch to attach the Bearer header and unwrap the Step 3 success envelope. The shared types module mirrors the backend domain (user, product, cart, order) so pages stay type-safe, while AuthContext provides login, register, logout, and current-user state and I18nContext supplies the active EN/FR dictionary. Every storefront page in Step 10 builds on these four modules.
title: Storefront API Bridge

description: The localized [lang] route tree renders the shopper journey: the products page lists the Step 5 catalog with add-to-cart actions, the cart page edits quantities and checks out into a Step 7 order, the orders page shows purchase history with totals, and the admin products page exposes create, edit, and delete flows. The locale layout validates the language, loads its dictionary, and wires the Step 9 auth and i18n providers around every page. Locale routing itself is handled by the proxy resolving cookie or Accept-Language headers.
title: Storefront Shopping Journey

description: To cap the tour, the Postman collection documents runnable auth, users, products, cart, and order requests with JWT usage notes, and its environment pins the base_url to the local NestJS server from Step 2. BACKEND_RULES.md is the strict contract behind those calls: the success envelope, error shapes, guard pipeline, and Prisma transaction guarantees from Steps 3-7. Use these two artifacts to exercise everything you just learned end to end.
title: API Contract Verification
